questions.question: Why did you move into development?
questions.answer: I majored in Library & Information Science and worked on a people database at Yonhap News, then in QA and CX at a logistics startup and at Fitogether. I cut a response form down to a single page, raised the opt-in profile submission rate by 30%, and lowered communication costs with a shared glossary — and that's when I realized what I love is shaping information so it's easy for people to use. But QA and CX were roles where I proposed improvements and handed them off; the more I did it, the more I wanted to build and fix things myself. I'd been coding since 2020, so moving into development felt natural.

questions.question: You're not a CS major — how did you build your fundamentals?
questions.answer: Library & Information Science is the study of classifying and structuring information, so my instinct for data modeling and consistent terminology actually comes from my major. I started coding there too, through courses like Information Technology (Python) and Software Programming, and I fill the gaps by building things myself. I implemented a TrueType font writer from scratch in pure Swift and published shared components as an npm library (formkit-react). My quality-engineering theory is backed by the ISTQB and CSTS certifications.

questions.question: How does your SQA/CX background help in frontend work?
questions.answer: Doing SQA and CX at two companies, I watched first-hand where users get confused and drop off, and that experience lives on in my code. I split errors into the predictable (400/422) and the unpredictable (5xx/network) and handle each by policy, and I apply performance strategies like virtualization against numeric thresholds — kicking in at 50 items, for example. Setting up issue trackers, unifying terminology, and building design systems are habits I picked up back then too.

questions.question: What are you working on now?
questions.answer: I'm a full-stack developer on Doppket, a digital-asset marketplace at Dost11, MBC's AI strategy subsidiary. I've owned Korean-market localization, the product dashboard, the blog CMS, and the checkout UX, and I led onboarding for our first B2B client. I turned a photobooth feature I pitched in a meeting into a prototype in three days, and I redesigned the UI/UX of a broadcast CG compositing tool side by side with ML researchers in a shared repo.

questions.question: How do you use AI tools?
questions.answer: Heavily — but I verify rather than trust blindly. At Chainshift I built three dashboard pages in seven days with Claude Code to support a sales demo, and I published a config that injects my code style and working rules into Claude Code. Conversely, on a hiring assignment I replaced AI-generated code with code I wrote myself to unify error handling, and documented the process in an analysis writeup. I also work with AI inside products — a few-shot font-generation pipeline and an ML monorepo.

questions.question: What matters most to you when collaborating?
questions.answer: I work PR-first and automate code quality with ESLint and Prettier plus Git hooks like Overcommit and Husky. I also look after quality outside the code — standardizing UI terms (e.g., visits/views collapsed into one 'views' label) and documenting responsive guidelines. At Dost11, research code and product code grew fast in one repo and screen wording and error messages drifted apart; I proposed aligning all user-facing text to one standard and unified everything myself, from screen labels to error messages across 50-some backend files. I write the accompanying tests, too.
